newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE - Ramos, from back seat to driver's seat.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ramos, from back seat to driver's seat.

text.p: As a young West Point cadet in the late 1940s, Fidel Ramos was once made to sit at the back of a bus in the southern United States because of his colour.

That young cadet is now firmly in the driving seat as Philippine head of state and U.S. President Bill Clinton and other Asia-Pacific leaders will be making courtesy calls on him in November when they gather here for a summit.
Ramos, a workaholic credited with midwifing the Philippines' economic rebirth, will chair the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit at Subic Bay, north of Manila, on November 25.

The summit crowns a career that has taken him from commander of an infantry platoon during the Korean War, where 40 of his West Point classmates were killed, to battling insurgents at home, to a stint in Vietnam with a Philippine Civic Action Group, to chief of staff of the Philippine armed forces, to defence minister and finally to the presidential palace.

At 68, Ramos still sets a pace that leaves his staff exhausted and has them in awe at his attention to detail and his occasional eruptions of anger. "He never rests. He misses nothing," said one senior aide.
This energy has helped drag the Philippines out of what Ramos describes as the "black pit of economic depression" into which it slid under the late former president Ferdinand Marcos.

From zero growth when Ramos took office in 1992 and a power crisis which saw most of the country without electricity for hours every day, the Philippines grew a respectable 7.1 percent in gross national product terms in the first half of 1996 and has seen a resurgence of foreign investment.

Ramos's policies, including a broad range of liberalisations from foreign exchange to the retail sector, have laid solid foundations for steady, sustainable growth, according to studies by the International Monetary Fund and private economists.

In an interview, Ramos recalls wryly how he was ordered to the back of the bus, a humiliation routinely inflicted on non-whites in the southern United States before the civil rights movement ended blatant discrimination.
"But my classmates, to their credit, got me out. They argued with the bus conductor and had me sit in front with them," he said.
Ramos graduated from the U.S. Military Academy in 1950 among the top of his class. He credits his gruelling four years there with instilling in him discipline and physical stamina.

Despite what his staff believe, he insists he does rest, and jokes that he once confessed to former president Corazon Aquino that he took occasional catnaps during cabinet meetings when he was her defence secretary.
He enjoys strenuous exercise and is a keen scuba diver. He used to jog, "but my knees aren't that good anymore".

He concedes he sometimes loses his temper, especially at people who fail to do the meticulous preparation he insists on. The military phrase "completed staff work" could well serve as the motto for his administration -- it basically means "do your homework".
His anger passes quickly and he makes sure he apologises if he has unfairly hurt someone's feelings, he said. "I do very quickly subside and I carry no grudges."
Occasionally, his temper has caused problems with Manila's freewheeling press. "Maybe a word let out in the heat of temper becomes the basis of a media story, and that's not so good," he said.
Apart from the economic accomplishments of his government, Ramos said that after he steps down from office in 1998 he would above all like to be remembered as a peacemaker.
The government and Moslem rebels recently signed an accord ending a decades-old separatist revolt in the southern Philippines.
Ramos's 45-year military career helps explain the persistence with which his administration pursued this accord.
"It is usually the soldier who aspires and longs for peace, more than anyone else," Ramos said.

The president, who comes from a family long involved in public service, including a stint as foreign minister for his father, hopes that some of the problem-solving techniques he has applied in Manila can also be used to drive APEC forward.

It is time, he said, that the grouping of 18 diverse states and territories started to produce concrete results and it was part of the Philippines' task as this year's host to try to help that happen.

"We'll give it our best try. As we've overcome various challenges in the past, I'm very confident that we can do in the Philippines in 1996 what we set out to do as the new APEC hosts. I'm sure we can do it," he said.
